patent: Filed 1954-10-28 and issued 1957-04-02 to William Shockley, assigned to Bell Telephone Laboratories. It describes doping by ion implantation: a monoenergetic beam of impurity ions (boron into N-type germanium in the example) is accelerated through tens of kilovolts so that the ions come to rest at a set depth below the surface and form a thin buried layer of the opposite type, after which a low-temperature anneal repairs the lattice damage without letting the implanted atoms diffuse. The stated aim is a thinner transistor base, and so a higher upper frequency limit. In the preferred form the wafer already holds a P-N junction and the buried layer is formed in the N zone as a continuation of the P zone, so a contact to the P zone also reaches the thin base. The text sets this apart from R. S. Ohl's earlier proposal (application Serial No. 141,152, which the text says issued as US 2,750,411) of bombarding a semiconductor surface to change its conductivity. Ion implantation became the standard way to introduce dopants in silicon integrated-circuit manufacture from the 1970s. Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Bardeen and Walter Brattain for their research on semiconductors and discovery of the transistor effect.

figs.1: Section through the glass apparatus, drawn upright; the underlined 20 names the whole envelope. Anode 31, a small block hung on wire 40 from lead-in 27 at the top, sits inside reentrant tube 34, whose lower end is closed by cathode 32 with its bore 38. Ions pass through 38 and down bombardment chamber 24 to wafer 25, which rests on base 49 of work holder 26; axial conductor 48 runs from the base down toward lead-in 29 at the bottom. Side arm 22 admits the boron trifluoride, side arm 21 goes to the pump and side arm 28 carries the cathode lead-in. Dashed lines in the stems are the lead-in wires. The deflection system the text mentions is not drawn.
figs.2A: Wafer 25 after bombardment, in perspective. The beam strikes the front (hatched) face, whose left half is N zone 25A and right half P zone 25B; the hatching direction marks the conductivity type (rising to the right for N, falling for P), while the stippling appears on every zone. Dashed lines on the top face trace the layers inside the N half: a thin N zone 25C at the front face, the bombarded P layer 25E behind it, and the remaining N zone 25D; 25E meets 25B and is continuous with it. Line 2B-2B on the front face gives the plane of FIG. 2B.
figs.2B: Section on line 2B-2B, with the beam arriving from the left. From the bombarded surface inward: the thin N zone 25C, the P layer 25E at the ion range, and N zone 25D, an N-P-N stack; layer widths are schematic. The text puts the emitter and collector contacts on 25C and 25D and the base contact on 25B, which lies outside this section.

glossary.def: Introducing dopant atoms into a crystal by firing accelerated ions into it; the accelerating voltage sets how deep they stop and the beam current and time set how many enter. The patent calls it ionic bombardment.
The patent's term for a dopant: an element that takes a lattice site in the semiconductor and contributes a free charge carrier.

A donor (five valence electrons, e.g. phosphorus or arsenic in germanium) gives an electron and makes N-type material; an acceptor (three, e.g. boron or aluminum) leaves a hole and makes P-type material.
Semiconductor doped with donors (N), so that electrons carry the current, or with acceptors (P), so that holes do.

A transistor of three zones, emitter, base and collector, in which the thin middle zone (base) is of the opposite type to the outer two. Carriers injected by the emitter diffuse across the base, so a thinner base gives a shorter transit time and a higher usable frequency.
An ion beam in which all ions have the same kinetic energy, so that they stop at about the same depth and the implanted layer stays thin.

Ions passing through the crystal knock atoms out of their lattice sites. Heating the wafer (here typically 400 C for ten minutes) lets the lattice reorder; the temperature is kept low enough that the implanted atoms barely diffuse.
BF_{3}, a gas used here as the source of boron ions; its ionization also yields ions of boron-fluorine compounds.
Here an arc discharge between anode and cathode in the gas-filled ion chamber; ions escape through holes in the cathode and are then accelerated toward the wafer.
Sorting ions by mass and charge in electric or magnetic fields, which the text suggests for removing unwanted ion species and charge states from the beam.
Electrostatic or magnetic lenses that focus and image ion beams, as electron optics do for electrons; the text uses them to project a reduced image of an apertured mask.
Grinding a surface flat with a fine abrasive on a plate.
A metal-to-semiconductor contact with linear, symmetric resistance, rather than a rectifying one.
A junction transistor with a second base connection; a bias between the two base contacts confines conduction to part of the base and improves high-frequency performance.
Semiconductors made of an element of group III and one of group V of the periodic table, such as indium antimonide.
